slides.title: Vectors, dot products and similarity
slides.text: Session 1 Vectors, dot products and similarity Compute a dot product, a norm and a cosine by hand and in NumPy Explain why cosine compares directions and ignores length Describe how distances behave as the dimension grows 01

slides.title: A vector is a point and an arrow at the same time
slides.text: Block A · vectors A vector is a point and an arrow at the same time A point: a data record A learner's week as (videos, quizzes, posts) = (1, 2, 2). Each coordinate is one measured quantity. An arrow: a direction The same numbers drawn from the origin. Its direction says the mix of activity; its length says how much. Order matters. (1, 2, 2) and (2, 1, 2) hold the same numbers and are different vectors: the coordinates are named positions.

slides.title: Adding vectors adds coordinates; scaling stretches the arrow
slides.text: Two operations Adding vectors adds coordinates; scaling stretches the arrow Operation Example Result Geometry Sum (1, 2, 2) + (2, 1, 2) (3, 3, 4) Head to tail Scale 3 × (1, 2, 2) (3, 6, 6) Same direction, three times as long Difference (2, 1, 2) − (1, 2, 2) (1, −1, 0) The arrow from the first point to the second In NumPy each line is one expression on arrays: x + y, 3 * x, y - x.

slides.title: The norm is the length of the arrow
slides.text: The norm The norm is the length of the arrow ‖x‖ = √(x₁² + x₂² + x₃²) , Pythagoras in three dimensions. For x = (1, 2, 2): ‖x‖ = √(1 + 4 + 4) = √9 = 3. The distance between two points is the norm of their difference: ‖y − x‖ = ‖(1, −1, 0)‖ = √2 ≈ 1.41. Units A norm adds squares of coordinates. If one coordinate is minutes and another is counts, the minutes dominate. Scale before you measure.

slides.title: Which learner is nearest?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which learner is nearest? Learners are vectors of (video minutes, quizzes). Learner K is (300, 2). Which is nearest to K by Euclidean distance: M (305, 9), N (330, 2) or P (290, 2)? P, because it matches K exactly on quizzes N, because its only difference is in one coordinate M, at a distance of about 8.6 None: minutes and quizzes cannot be combined in one distance

slides.title: The dot product multiplies matching coordinates and adds them
slides.text: Block B · the dot product The dot product multiplies matching coordinates and adds them x = (1, 2, 2), y = (2, 1, 2) x · y = 1×2 + 2×1 + 2×2 = 8 And x · x = 1 + 4 + 4 = 9 = ‖x‖²: the norm is a dot product with itself. x = np.array([1, 2, 2]) y = np.array([2, 1, 2]) x @ y # 8 np.sqrt(x @ x) # 3.0

slides.title: x · y = ‖x‖ ‖y‖ cos θ: the dot product measures an angle
slides.text: Geometry x · y = ‖x‖ ‖y‖ cos θ: the dot product measures an angle For our pair: cos θ = 8 / (3 × 3) = 0.889, so θ ≈ 27.3°. The cosine similarity is that cosine: the dot product of the two vectors after each is scaled to length 1. 0.889 cosine of (1, 2, 2) and (2, 1, 2)

slides.title: The sign of a dot product says acute, right or obtuse
slides.text: Reading the sign The sign of a dot product says acute, right or obtuse Pair Dot product Angle Reading (1, 0) and (1, 1) 1 45° Pointing the same way, partly (1, 0) and (0, 1) 0 90° Orthogonal: nothing in common (1, 0) and (−1, 1) −1 135° Pointing partly opposite Orthogonal means dot product zero. It comes back in every week from week 4 on.

slides.title: Cosine ignores length; the dot product does not
slides.text: Length or direction Cosine ignores length; the dot product does not x and 3x x · 3x = 27, larger than x · y = 8. Yet cos(x, 3x) = 1: the same direction exactly. Why a search cares A long document has a long vector. Ranking by raw dot product would favour length over meaning. Cosine compares only direction.

slides.title: A matrix times a vector is many dot products at once
slides.text: At scale A matrix times a vector is many dot products at once D = np.array([[1, 2, 2], [2, 1, 2], [3, 6, 6]], float) N = D / np.linalg.norm(D, axis=1, keepdims=True) q = np.array([1, 2, 2]) / 3 N @ q # [1.0, 0.889, 1.0] Each row of D is one item; normalise every row to length 1 N @ q gives the cosine of the question with every row The best match is the largest entry: np.argmax

slides.title: Dot product or cosine?
slides.text: Checkpoint Dot product or cosine? A question vector q = (1, 1). Two help articles: A = (4, 4) and B = (1, 1.2). Which statement is right? A is closer in direction, since q · A = 8 beats q · B = 2.2 A and q differ in direction, since A is four times longer Both measures rank A first, so the choice never matters A has cosine 1 with q and B a little less; the dot product also rewards A's length

slides.title: An embedding places words so that related words point the same way
slides.text: Block C · embeddings An embedding places words so that related words point the same way A model reads a large text collection and gives each word a vector Words used in similar contexts get vectors at small angles The course uses GloVe: 400,000 words, 50 numbers each, trained on 6 billion tokens of encyclopedia and news text Licence The pre-trained GloVe vectors are released under the Public Domain Dedication and License. The lab downloads them; nothing is copied into the course.

slides.title: Here a sentence vector is the mean of its word vectors
slides.text: From words to sentences Here a sentence vector is the mean of its word vectors 1 · Split "video will not play" into four words → 2 · Look up four GloVe vectors of 50 numbers → 3 · Average one vector of 50 numbers for the sentence A baseline, not a sentence model. The mean ignores word order and is pulled by frequent words. It is the simplest public sentence embedding, and the lab measures how far it gets.

slides.title: When every vector shares a big common part, every cosine looks high
slides.text: A shared direction When every vector shares a big common part, every cosine looks high Toy vectors Pair cosines (6, 4), (4, 6), (6, 6) 0.923, 0.981, 0.981 After subtracting their mean −0.800, −0.316, −0.316 The three share the part (5, 5); their differences are small Centring subtracts the mean vector and leaves the differences After centring, angles describe how the items differ

slides.title: In many dimensions, the nearest and the farthest point come close
slides.text: High dimensions In many dimensions, the nearest and the farthest point come close 2 dimensions 58.69 10 dimensions 3.49 100 dimensions 0.46 1,000 dimensions 0.13 Contrast = (farthest − nearest) / nearest, from one random point to 499 others with independent standard normal coordinates.

slides.title: Vectors learn the associations of the text they were trained on
slides.text: What the vectors learnt Vectors learn the associations of the text they were trained on The lean of a word w between two word lists: lean(w) = mean of cos(w, female word) − cos(w, male word), over pairs such as she/he and woman/man. Positive: closer to the female words. Zero: no lean. Why it matters A search that matches a learner's free-text goal to courses through these vectors inherits their leans. The lab measures them; whether a search treats learners differently must be tested on the search.

slides.title: Reading a search score
slides.text: Checkpoint Reading a search score A search over mean word vectors returns two articles with cosines 0.951 and 0.949 to a question. What is the soundest reading? The scores barely differ; check whether a shared direction inflates every cosine before trusting the order Both are excellent matches, since a cosine above 0.9 means near-identical meaning The first article is clearly the better answer, since it scores higher There is a 95% chance that either article answers the question

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Week 1 · wrap-up Three things to keep Length and angle The norm is a length; the dot product divided by two lengths is the cosine of an angle. Centre first A direction every vector shares makes every cosine high. Subtract the mean before comparing. Vectors carry text Embeddings inherit the associations of their training text. Measure them before building on them.

slides.title: Entry (i, j) of AB is row i of A dotted with column j of B
slides.text: Block A · the product Entry (i, j) of AB is row i of A dotted with column j of B P = [[2, 1], [1, 3]] (2 × 2), G = [[1, 0, 1], [2, 1, 0]] (2 × 3) Entry (1, 1): (2, 1) · (1, 2) = 4 P G = [[4, 1, 2], [7, 3, 1]] , a 2 × 3 matrix Shapes first (n × k)(k × m) gives n × m. The inner sizes must match. G P does not exist here: 3 does not match 2.

slides.title: Stacking vectors as rows turns all their dot products into one product
slides.text: Many dot products Stacking vectors as rows turns all their dot products into one product Questions as rows of Q (q × d), articles as rows of A (a × d) Q Aᵀ is q × a: entry (i, j) is question i dotted with article j Week 1's search for one question was one row of this matrix Why it matters. One product call replaces q × a separate dot products, and the computer runs it far faster.

slides.title: Attention scores are a matrix of dot products, scaled and softened
slides.text: Attention Attention scores are a matrix of dot products, scaled and softened 1 · Scores S = Q Kᵀ / √d → 2 · Softmax each row to positive weights adding to 1 → 3 · Mix weights times the value vectors One query q = (1, 0) against keys (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1) with d = 2: scores 0.707, 0, 0.707; weights 0.401, 0.198, 0.401.

slides.title: The shape of the scores
slides.text: Checkpoint The shape of the scores A layer compares 12 queries with 30 keys, each vector of length 64. What is the shape of S = Q Kᵀ? 30 × 12 12 × 64 12 × 30 64 × 64

slides.title: A matrix is a map: it sends each vector to a new vector
slides.text: Block B · maps A matrix is a map: it sends each vector to a new vector Its columns are where the axis vectors land Rot = [[0, −1], [1, 0]] sends (1, 0) to (0, 1): a quarter turn Ref = [[1, 0], [0, −1]] flips the second coordinate: a mirror Read the columns To know what a 2 × 2 matrix does, draw where (1, 0) and (0, 1) go. Every other vector follows by adding and scaling.

slides.title: A product of matrices is one map applied after another, read right to left
slides.text: Composition A product of matrices is one map applied after another, read right to left Matrix Means Sends (1, 1) to Ref Rot turn first, then mirror (−1, −1) Rot Ref mirror first, then turn (1, 1) Order matters. Ref Rot ≠ Rot Ref. Matrix products are not commutative, because doing two things in another order is another map.

slides.title: Stacked linear layers compose into one matrix
slides.text: In machine learning Stacked linear layers compose into one matrix Two linear layers W₂(W₁ x) equal one layer (W₂ W₁) x Without a non-linear step between them, depth adds nothing Shapes chain: (m × h)(h × d) maps d inputs to m outputs Cost still counts. W₂(W₁ x) and (W₂ W₁) x give the same result with different numbers of operations. Block C counts them.

slides.title: Which matrix does "scale, then turn"?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which matrix does "scale, then turn"? S doubles every vector's first coordinate; T turns the plane a quarter turn. You want one matrix that scales first, then turns. Which is it? T S S T S + T S T or T S, which are equal

slides.title: An (n × k)(k × m) product costs 2·n·k·m floating-point operations
slides.text: Block C · cost An (n × k)(k × m) product costs 2·n·k·m floating-point operations n·m entries, each a dot product of length k: k multiplications and k additions. (3 × 4)(4 × 2): 2 × 3 × 4 × 2 = 48 FLOPs. n FLOPs of n × n times n × n MB per matrix 100 0.002 G 0.08 1,000 2 G 8 10,000 2,000 G 800

slides.title: Where you put the brackets changes the cost, not the answer
slides.text: Same result, different bill Where you put the brackets changes the cost, not the answer Order FLOPs (W₂ W₁) x, with W₂ 10 × 1,000, W₁ 1,000 × 1,000, x of length 1,000 20,020,000 W₂ (W₁ x) 2,020,000 2·10·1,000·1,000 + 2·10·1,000 against 2·1,000·1,000 + 2·10·1,000.

slides.title: A Python loop pays for every number; a vectorised call pays once
slides.text: A first look at vectorisation A Python loop pays for every number; a vectorised call pays once # loop: one Python step per multiply for i in range(n): for j in range(m): C[i][j] = sum(A[i][t] * B[t][j] for t in range(k)) # vectorised: one call C = A @ B Same arithmetic, same FLOP count The call runs compiled code over whole blocks of memory Week 8 returns to vectorisation and broadcasting in full

slides.title: The span of some vectors is everything you can build from them
slides.text: Block A · span The span of some vectors is everything you can build from them A combination of u and v is a u + b v, for any numbers a and b The span is the set of all combinations: a line, a plane, or more (1, 2) and (2, 4) span only a line: the second is twice the first (1, 0) and (0, 1) span the whole plane For data. The columns of a feature table span the set of predictions any linear model on them can make.

slides.title: Vectors are independent when none is a combination of the others
slides.text: Independence Vectors are independent when none is a combination of the others Independent The only combination that gives zero is all coefficients zero. Each vector adds a new direction. Dependent Some combination with non-zero coefficients gives zero: 2(1, 2) − (2, 4) = (0, 0). One vector repeats the others. A basis of a span is an independent set that spans it. Every basis of the same span has the same size: that size is the dimension.

slides.title: The rank is the number of independent columns, and also of independent rows
slides.text: Rank The rank is the number of independent columns, and also of independent rows Course Hours Minutes Lessons Course 1 2 120 8 Course 2 3 180 10 Course 3 1 60 5 Course 4 4 240 12 Minutes = 60 × hours exactly Three columns, rank 2 Singular values 329.18, 2.51 and 0: one direction is missing

slides.text: Checkpoint How many features are really there? A table has columns: price, tax (15% of price), price with tax, and a discount code that varies freely. What is its rank, if there are many rows? 4 2 3 1

slides.title: Solving A x = b asks which combination of A's columns makes b
slides.text: Block B · linear systems Solving A x = b asks which combination of A's columns makes b One solution b is in the span and the columns are independent. Infinitely many b is in the span and the columns are dependent: one solution plus any null-space vector. None b is outside the span. Week 5 finds the closest combination instead.

slides.title: Elimination subtracts rows until the system is a staircase
slides.text: Elimination Elimination subtracts rows until the system is a staircase Step Rows of [A | b] Start [2, 1, 1 | 4], [4, 3, 3 | 10], [8, 7, 9 | 24] Row 2 − 2 × row 1; row 3 − 4 × row 1 [2, 1, 1 | 4], [0, 1, 1 | 2], [0, 3, 5 | 8] Row 3 − 3 × row 2 [2, 1, 1 | 4], [0, 1, 1 | 2], [0, 0, 2 | 2] Back substitution from the bottom: z = 1, then y = 1, then x = 1.

slides.title: A zero or tiny pivot breaks elimination; swapping rows fixes most cases
slides.text: Pivots A zero or tiny pivot breaks elimination; swapping rows fixes most cases The pivot is the number you divide by at each step A zero pivot with nothing to swap in means a dependent column: the matrix is singular A tiny pivot magnifies rounding; partial pivoting swaps in the row with the largest entry The number of non-zero pivots is the rank

slides.title: What does a zero pivot tell you?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does a zero pivot tell you? Elimination on a 4 × 4 matrix finds no non-zero pivot in the third column, even after looking for a row to swap. What follows? The computation needs more precision The system has exactly one solution, found by skipping the column The columns are dependent; the system has no solution or infinitely many The right-hand side b must be zero

slides.title: The inverse undoes a map, and exists only when nothing was lost
slides.text: Block C · the inverse The inverse undoes a map, and exists only when nothing was lost [[4, 7], [2, 6]] has determinant 4 × 6 − 7 × 2 = 10, so inverse = [[0.6, −0.7], [−0.2, 0.4]] Check: multiply them and get the identity. No inverse A singular matrix squashes some direction to zero. Nothing can bring it back: two inputs give the same output.

slides.title: To solve a system, call a solver; do not invert and multiply
slides.text: In code To solve a system, call a solver; do not invert and multiply x = np.linalg.solve(A, b) # yes x = np.linalg.inv(A) @ b # avoid Solving does less work than inverting It rounds less, and the gap grows with the condition number You rarely need the inverse itself

slides.title: On a computer, "zero" means "small compared with rounding"
slides.text: Rounding On a computer, "zero" means "small compared with rounding" A float64 number holds about 16 significant digits Exact dependence shows as a singular value of rounding size, about 10⁻¹⁶ times the largest or less, not always exactly 0 np.linalg.matrix_rank counts singular values above a tolerance set from the matrix's size and largest value Near, not exact. A column that almost repeats another keeps the rank full and still makes a solve unstable. Weeks 4 and 5 measure that.

slides.text: Checkpoint Can this table be inverted? A 3 × 3 matrix has rows (1, 2, 3), (0, 1, 4) and (1, 3, 7). Does it have an inverse? Yes: no row is all zeros Yes: no two rows are equal It depends on the vector b it is used with No: the third row is the sum of the first two

slides.title: The projection is the nearest point on the line, and the residual meets it at a right angle
slides.text: Block A · projection onto a line The projection is the nearest point on the line, and the residual meets it at a right angle p = (b · a / a · a) a b = (2, 4), a = (3, 1): b · a = 10, a · a = 10, so p = (3, 1). Residual b − p = (−1, 3), and (−1, 3) · (3, 1) = 0. Why a right angle If the residual leaned along the line, sliding the point that way would bring it closer. The nearest point leaves only the orthogonal part.

slides.title: Onto the span of several columns, the projection matrix is A (AᵀA)⁻¹ Aᵀ
slides.text: Onto a subspace Onto the span of several columns, the projection matrix is A (AᵀA)⁻¹ Aᵀ A with columns (1, 0, 1) and (0, 1, 1); v = (1, 2, 0) P v = (0, 1, 1), residual (1, 1, −1) The residual is orthogonal to both columns: (1, 1, −1) · (1, 0, 1) = 0 and · (0, 1, 1) = 0. Condition: Aᵀ(v − P v) = 0, the normal equations Compute it with a solve, never an inverse

slides.title: Projecting twice changes nothing, and a projection matrix is symmetric
slides.text: Two properties Projecting twice changes nothing, and a projection matrix is symmetric P² = P A point already on the subspace stays where it is. Pᵀ = P An orthogonal projection treats both sides alike. A projection that is not symmetric projects at a slant. Use them as checks. If your P fails either, the code is wrong. The lab and the problem set test both.

slides.title: Where does the projection land?
slides.text: Checkpoint Where does the projection land? Project b = (4, 2) onto the line through a = (1, 0). Which is the projection, and why? (0, 2), the part along the second axis (4, 0), since b · a / a · a = 4 (4), the number b · a (0.894, 0), the unit vector of b on the axis

slides.title: With an orthonormal basis, projecting is just dot products
slides.text: Block B · orthonormal bases With an orthonormal basis, projecting is just dot products Orthonormal : unit length, pairwise orthogonal: QᵀQ = I Projection onto their span: P = Q Qᵀ, no solve needed The coordinates of v are simply the dot products qᵢ · v The plan. Turn any independent columns into orthonormal ones with the same span. That is Gram-Schmidt, and the bookkeeping is the QR factorisation.

slides.title: Gram-Schmidt removes from each column what earlier columns already explain
slides.text: Gram-Schmidt Gram-Schmidt removes from each column what earlier columns already explain Columns (3, 4) and (1, 0) Result q₁ = (3, 4) / 5 (0.6, 0.8) Coefficient r₁₂ = q₁ · (1, 0) 0.6 What is left: (1, 0) − 0.6 q₁ (0.64, −0.48), length 0.8 q₂ = what is left / 0.8 (0.8, −0.6)

slides.title: A = Q R: Q holds the orthonormal columns, R the coefficients
slides.text: The factorisation A = Q R: Q holds the orthonormal columns, R the coefficients For the example: R = [[5, 0.6], [0, 0.8]] Column 1 of A = 5 q₁; column 2 = 0.6 q₁ + 0.8 q₂. Q, R = np.linalg.qr(A) np.allclose(Q.T @ Q, np.eye(2)) # True np.allclose(Q @ R, A) # True Signs. A library may return −q and −r for some columns. Both are correct: QR is unique only up to those signs.

slides.title: Which check proves your QR is right?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which check proves your QR is right? Your function returns Q (5 × 3) and R (3 × 3) for a 5 × 3 matrix A. Which set of checks is enough? QᵀQ = I Q R = A Q equals np.linalg.qr(A)[0] entry by entry QᵀQ = I, Q R = A and R upper triangular

slides.title: When columns are nearly parallel, subtracting shadows leaves mostly rounding
slides.text: Block C · rounding When columns are nearly parallel, subtracting shadows leaves mostly rounding Two columns at a tiny angle: almost all of the second is its shadow on the first What is left is small, and rounding errors are a large part of it Classical Gram-Schmidt projects the original column each time; modified projects the updated one, and keeps more accuracy Libraries use Householder reflections, which keep Q orthonormal to rounding level

slides.title: A Q that is not orthonormal gives wrong projections without any error message
slides.text: Why it matters A Q that is not orthonormal gives wrong projections without any error message Silent failure Q Qᵀ v is a projection only if QᵀQ = I. Code that skips the check returns numbers that look fine. The habit After any factorisation, measure max |QᵀQ − I| and max |QR − A|. Both should be near 10⁻¹⁵ in float64.

slides.title: A measured loss of orthogonality
slides.text: Checkpoint A measured loss of orthogonality For a QR of a feature matrix you measure max |QᵀQ − I| = 0.02. What is the soundest next step? Suspect nearly dependent columns, check the condition number, and use a Householder QR Accept it: 0.02 is a small number Use fewer rows so the factorisation is faster and more accurate Normalise each column of Q again to length 1

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Week 4 · wrap-up Three things to keep Nearest means orthogonal The residual of a projection is orthogonal to the subspace: Aᵀ(v − P v) = 0. QR is projection bookkeeping Q spans the same space with orthonormal columns; R records how to rebuild A. Measure the loss Check max |QᵀQ − I| after every factorisation; prefer Householder.

slides.title: With more data points than unknowns, there is usually no exact solution
slides.text: Block A · least squares With more data points than unknowns, there is usually no exact solution Three points, a line with two coefficients: X β = y has no solution unless the points line up Least squares chooses β to make ‖y − X β‖ as small as possible X β ranges over the span of the columns, so the best X β is the projection of y onto it So: the residual y − X β is orthogonal to every column: Xᵀ(y − X β) = 0.

slides.title: XᵀX β = Xᵀy: least squares by hand
slides.text: The normal equations XᵀX β = Xᵀy: least squares by hand Points (−1, 1), (0, 1), (1, 4); X = [1, x] XᵀX = [[3, 0], [0, 2]], Xᵀy = (6, 3) β = (2, 1.5) : y ≈ 2 + 1.5x Check the residual Fitted (0.5, 2, 3.5), residual (0.5, −1, 0.5). It sums to zero and is orthogonal to x: Xᵀr = (0, 0).

slides.title: With X = QR, least squares becomes a triangular solve: R β = Qᵀy
slides.text: The QR route With X = QR, least squares becomes a triangular solve: R β = Qᵀy Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X) beta = solve_triangular(R, Q.T @ y) # the library's own route (SVD) beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0] Q Qᵀ y is the projection of y; Qᵀy its coordinates XᵀX is never formed Back substitution, as in week 3

slides.title: Which fit is the least-squares fit?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which fit is the least-squares fit? Two candidate fits for the same data. Fit F has residual (1, −2, 1) and fit G has residual (2, −1, −1). The columns of X are (1, 1, 1) and (−1, 0, 1). Which can be the least-squares fit? G, because its residual is more even F, because its residual is orthogonal to both columns Both, since their residuals have the same length Neither, because neither residual is zero

slides.title: The condition number says how much a small change in the data can move the answer
slides.text: Block B · conditioning The condition number says how much a small change in the data can move the answer A = [[1, 1], [1, 1.0001]], cond(A) ≈ 4 × 10⁴ b Solution of A x = b (2, 2.0001) (1, 1) (2, 2.0002) (0, 2) Rule of thumb About log₁₀ cond decimal digits of accuracy are at risk. Float64 carries about 16.

slides.title: Forming XᵀX squares the condition number
slides.text: Why QR Forming XᵀX squares the condition number 4 × 10⁴ cond(A) for the matrix of the last slide 1.6 × 10⁹ cond(AᵀA): about 9 of 16 digits at risk The normal equations work with cond(X)²; QR works with cond(X). For well-conditioned data both are fine. As columns approach collinearity, the normal equations fail first.

slides.title: Nearly collinear features make coefficients unstable and fitted values stable
slides.text: In data Nearly collinear features make coefficients unstable and fitted values stable Two columns that nearly repeat each other: many β give almost the same X β The fit barely changes when the data is nudged The split of the effect between the two columns can swing widely For the report. Do not read the coefficient of one of two nearly collinear features as "the effect" of that feature.

slides.title: Diagnose a fit
slides.text: Checkpoint Diagnose a fit A fit has cond(X) = 10⁷. Refitting after rounding the data to four decimals changes two coefficients by 30% and the fitted values by 0.01%. What is the diagnosis? The rounding was too coarse; the model is fine The model is stable, since its predictions hardly moved Ill-conditioned: nearly collinear columns; trust the fit, not those two coefficients Rank-deficient: one column must be removed before any fit

slides.title: Some ill-conditioning is only a matter of units
slides.text: Block C · what helps Some ill-conditioning is only a matter of units Cause What helps Columns on very different scales (metres and millimetres) Divide each column by its standard deviation A large mean far from zero, beside the intercept Centre each column Columns that nearly repeat each other Drop or combine one; scaling does not help Exactly repeated columns Drop one: the matrix is rank-deficient

slides.title: Prefer QR or the library's least-squares solver; check the condition number
slides.text: In practice Prefer QR or the library's least-squares solver; check the condition number Normal equations Fast and simple; squares the condition number. Fine when cond(X) is small. QR The default for full-rank problems: works with cond(X). SVD (lstsq) Slowest; handles rank deficiency by ignoring tiny singular values. Week 7.

slides.title: Which route for this fit?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which route for this fit? A feature matrix has cond(X) = 10⁶ in float64. You need coefficients accurate to at least six digits. Which route? The normal equations: they are fastest QR, which puts about 6 digits at risk and leaves about 10 The normal equations in float32 to save memory Invert XᵀX and multiply by Xᵀy

slides.title: An eigenvector is a direction the matrix only stretches
slides.text: Block A · eigenvectors An eigenvector is a direction the matrix only stretches A = [[4, 1], [1, 4]] A (1, 0) = (4, 1): turned, not an eigenvector A (1, 1) = (5, 5) = 5 × (1, 1): an eigenvector, eigenvalue 5 A v = λ v λ is the stretch factor. A negative λ flips the direction; λ = 0 squashes it: the matrix is singular.

slides.title: Eigenvalues solve det(A − λI) = 0
slides.text: By hand Eigenvalues solve det(A − λI) = 0 det([[4 − λ, 1], [1, 4 − λ]]) = (4 − λ)² − 1 = 0 4 − λ = ±1, so λ = 5 or 3 For a 2 × 2: λ² − (trace) λ + det = 0. Here trace 8, det 15. w, V = np.linalg.eigh(A) w # [3., 5.] ascending V[:, 1] # [0.7071, 0.7071]

slides.title: A symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors
slides.text: Symmetric matrices A symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors A = Q Λ Qᵀ: rotate into the eigenvector basis, stretch each axis, rotate back (1, 1)/√2 and (1, −1)/√2 are orthogonal, as week 4 would want Covariance matrices and XᵀX are symmetric: everything this week applies to them Machine learning use. The eigenvalues of XᵀX are the squares of X's singular values; their ratio is cond(X)², week 5's number.

slides.title: Reading eigenvalues
slides.text: Checkpoint Reading eigenvalues A symmetric 3 × 3 matrix has eigenvalues 9, 4 and 0. Which statement is right? Its diagonal entries are 9, 4 and 0 It is invertible, because two eigenvalues are positive It has rank 2 and squashes one direction to zero Its eigenvectors have lengths 9, 4 and 0

slides.title: A covariance matrix records how features vary together
slides.text: Block B · covariance A covariance matrix records how features vary together Learner Quiz 1 Quiz 2 1 60 65 2 70 72 3 80 79 4 90 88 5 50 56 Centre the columns (means 70 and 72), then C = XcᵀXc / (n − 1): C = [[250, 195], [195, 152.5]] Diagonal: variances. Off the diagonal: how the two move together.

slides.title: The leading eigenvector of the covariance is the direction of greatest spread
slides.text: Principal components The leading eigenvector of the covariance is the direction of greatest spread 99.94% of the total variance lies along (0.79, 0.62) Eigenvalues 402.25 and 0.25 The two quizzes are almost one measurement: "overall score" That direction is the first principal component Machine learning use. Principal component analysis (PCA) keeps the few directions that hold most of the variance. Week 7 computes it through the SVD.

slides.title: What does the first component tell you?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does the first component tell you? Four features of course pages have a covariance matrix with eigenvalues 30, 5, 1 and 0.5. What can you say? All four features carry about the same information About 82% of the variance lies along one direction, a combination of the features The first feature explains 82% of the variance The fourth feature is an error and must be removed

slides.title: Multiply by the matrix again and again, and the leading eigenvector wins
slides.text: Block C · power iteration Multiply by the matrix again and again, and the leading eigenvector wins Write the start as a mix of eigenvectors Each multiplication scales each part by its eigenvalue The part with the largest |λ| outgrows the rest; normalise to keep the numbers in range The error shrinks by about |λ₂ / λ₁| per step

slides.title: A page's rank is the chance a random reader is on it, in the long run
slides.text: Link ranking A page's rank is the chance a random reader is on it, in the long run Pages P, Q, R. P links to Q and R, Q to R, R to P. Column-stochastic M; start (1/3, 1/3, 1/3). Step P, Q, R 1 0.333, 0.167, 0.500 2 0.500, 0.167, 0.333 limit 0.4, 0.2, 0.4 An eigenvector The limit satisfies M x = x: the eigenvector of eigenvalue 1, scaled to add up to 1.

slides.title: Dead ends, closed loops and link farms break the plain walk; damping repairs it
slides.text: What goes wrong Dead ends, closed loops and link farms break the plain walk; damping repairs it Problem Effect Repair A page with no links out Probability leaks away Jump anywhere from it A closed group of pages The walk is trapped, may cycle Damping: jump anywhere with probability 1 − d Pages that link to each other to lift one The group gains rank Smaller d limits it; it does not remove it

slides.title: Why does damping speed up convergence?
slides.text: Checkpoint Why does damping speed up convergence? With damping d = 0.85, power iteration converges in about a hundred steps; at d = 0.99 it takes many more. Why? A larger d removes pages from the graph A larger d makes the leading eigenvalue larger than 1 A larger d needs a better starting vector The second-largest eigenvalue is at most d, so the error shrinks more slowly when d is near 1

slides.title: Every matrix is a rotation, a stretch along the axes, and another rotation
slides.text: Block A · the SVD Every matrix is a rotation, a stretch along the axes, and another rotation 1 · Vᵀ turn the input onto the axes → 2 · Σ stretch each axis by σᵢ ≥ 0 → 3 · U turn onto the output directions A = U Σ Vᵀ , for any m × n matrix. U and V have orthonormal columns; the singular values σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ … ≥ 0.

slides.title: The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA
slides.text: By hand The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA A = [[2, 2], [−1, 1]] AᵀA = [[5, 3], [3, 5]], eigenvalues 8 and 2 σ₁ = √8 ≈ 2.828, σ₂ = √2 ≈ 1.414 U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A) s # [2.8284, 1.4142] np.allclose(U @ np.diag(s) @ Vt, A)

slides.title: The singular values give rank, size and conditioning at a glance
slides.text: What it reveals The singular values give rank, size and conditioning at a glance Read off Σ Meaning Week Number of non-zero σ The rank 3 σ₁ The largest stretch: the matrix's 2-norm 7 σ₁ / σₙ The condition number 5 How fast σ falls How well a few layers summarise the matrix 7, 8

slides.title: Reading singular values
slides.text: Checkpoint Reading singular values A 500 × 40 feature matrix has singular values 310, 52, 9, … , 0.004, 0.000002. What does that tell you? All 40 directions are equally informative The condition number is 310 Full rank but nearly rank-deficient: cond ≈ 1.6 × 10⁸, unsafe for the normal equations The rank is 3

slides.title: A is a sum of rank-one layers, largest first: keep the first k
slides.text: Block B · low rank A is a sum of rank-one layers, largest first: keep the first k A = σ₁ u₁v₁ᵀ + σ₂ u₂v₂ᵀ + … A_k keeps the first k layers. Each layer is an outer product: one column pattern times one row pattern. Eckart-Young No rank-k matrix is closer to A than A_k, and ‖A − A_k‖²_F = σ²ₖ₊₁ + … + σ²ₙ. The error is known before you build A_k.

slides.title: Two layers rebuild this 4 × 3 matrix to within 8%
slides.text: A small case Two layers rebuild this 4 × 3 matrix to within 8% Rows of M (5, 4, 1) (4, 5, 1) (1, 1, 3) (5, 5, 1) k Relative error ‖M − M_k‖ / ‖M‖ 1 0.2398 2 0.0828 3 0 Singular values 11.73, 2.72 and 1.00: the error of each row is the tail of that list.

slides.title: A rank-k copy stores k(m + n + 1) numbers instead of m × n
slides.text: The trade A rank-k copy stores k(m + n + 1) numbers instead of m × n 4.5% storage of a rank-20 copy of a 1,000 × 800 matrix: 36,020 numbers of 800,000 Small k saves space only when the σ fall fast Past some k, the copy is larger than the matrix Choose k from the error curve, not by habit

slides.title: Predict the error before computing it
slides.text: Checkpoint Predict the error before computing it A matrix has singular values 10, 6, 3 and 1. What is ‖A − A₂‖_F, the error of its best rank-2 approximation? 3 4 √136 ≈ 11.66 √10 ≈ 3.16

slides.title: Centre the data, take its SVD: the rows of Vᵀ are the principal components
slides.text: Block C · PCA through the SVD Centre the data, take its SVD: the rows of Vᵀ are the principal components Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0) U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False) components = Vt # one per row share = s**2 / np.sum(s**2) # variance share scores = Xc @ Vt[:2].T # 2-D view Same as week 6's eigenvectors of the covariance Without forming the covariance, so better rounding σ² / (n − 1) are the variances along each component

slides.title: A component is a pattern of weights over the original features
slides.text: Interpreting A component is a pattern of weights over the original features For images: each component is itself an image; large weights mark pixels that vary together The sign is arbitrary: flip a component and its scores flip with it Look at which items score highest and lowest on it, then name what separates them A component explains variance, not meaning: interpretation is a claim to check

slides.title: A component that points at the mean
slides.text: Checkpoint A component that points at the mean A colleague takes the SVD of a ratings matrix without centring it. The first singular value is huge and the first right singular vector has nearly equal entries. What happened? slides.title: A ratings matrix is close to low rank because tastes are few
slides.text: Block A · recommenders A ratings matrix is close to low rank because tastes are few Rows are people, columns are items; most entries are missing A rank-k model: each person is k numbers of taste, each item k numbers of character A predicted rating is the dot product of the two Truncated SVD after filling the gaps is the simplest version; methods that fit only the observed entries do better

slides.title: Choose the rank on ratings the model did not see
slides.text: Choosing k Choose the rank on ratings the model did not see Training error Falls with every extra layer, down to zero at full rank. It cannot choose k. Held-out error Falls, then rises once extra layers fit noise. Its lowest point is the rank to use. The trap. Choosing k on the test set and then reporting the test error flatters the model. With enough data, keep a third split for the final report.

slides.title: A low-rank update adapts a large model by training two thin matrices
slides.text: Model adaptation A low-rank update adapts a large model by training two thin matrices W' = W + B A, with B d × r and A r × d, W frozen d = 1,024, r = 8: 16,384 trainable numbers against 1,048,576: 1.56% Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) The 2021 paper that introduced the method reports up to 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters on its largest model.

slides.title: Broadcasting lines shapes up from the right and stretches dimensions of 1
slides.text: Block B · vectorisation and broadcasting Broadcasting lines shapes up from the right and stretches dimensions of 1 (3, 1) + (1, 2) gives (3, 2): a = np.array([[1], [2], [3]]) # (3, 1) b = np.array([[10, 20]]) # (1, 2) a + b # [[11, 21], [12, 22], [13, 23]] Compare shapes from the last dimension Equal sizes match; a size of 1 stretches Anything else is an error

slides.title: A square test matrix hides an axis bug
slides.text: Silent errors A square test matrix hides an axis bug M - M.mean(axis=1) on an n × m matrix lines the row means up with the columns If n ≠ m it fails with an error; if n = m it runs and is wrong Use keepdims=True, or a shape that says what you mean: (n, 1) Test with rectangular shapes, such as 2 × 3, never only square ones

slides.text: Checkpoint Predict the shape X has shape (100, 5). What does X - X.mean(axis=0) do? Subtracts each row's mean from that row Raises a shape error Subtracts one overall mean from every entry Subtracts each column's mean from that column

slides.title: A float keeps a fixed number of significant digits, about 7 or 16
slides.text: Block C · floating point A float keeps a fixed number of significant digits, about 7 or 16 Expression Result Why 1e16 + 1 − 1e16 0.0 At 10¹⁶ the gap between float64 numbers is 2 float32: 1 + 10⁻⁸ == 1 True Machine epsilon for float32 is 1.19 × 10⁻⁷ Subtracting nearly equal numbers Most digits cancel What is left is mostly rounding

slides.title: Trust code that agrees with a hand case and a trusted library, within a stated tolerance
slides.text: Checking code Trust code that agrees with a hand case and a trusted library, within a stated tolerance 1 · Hand case a 2 × 2 or 2 × 3 you worked on paper → 2 · Properties Qᵀ Q = I, A x = b, rows sum to zero → 3 · Random cases against the library, with a tolerance Tolerance. Compare with np.allclose(a, b, atol, rtol), never with ==. State the tolerance you chose and why.

slides.title: Why does this test fail?
slides.text: Checkpoint Why does this test fail? A test asserts Q.T @ Q == np.eye(3) for a correct QR and fails. What is wrong? Exact equality on floats: compare with a tolerance instead The QR routine has a bug The product should be Q @ Q.T Convert Q to float32 first
